email.scenario: Last week you attended an evening talk at your town's heritage society, where a retired tannery foreman, Mr. Aldous Finch, described working life at the old tannery. You lead a weekend walking group of thirty members, and next spring the group will follow a heritage walk that passes the tannery yard. You have never met Mr. Finch, but you would like him to give the same talk at the group's spring meeting, which could be held on either of two Saturdays.
email.subject: Invitation to repeat your tannery talk for our walking group
bullets: Tell Mr. Finch what you appreciated about his talk on the old tannery.
Invite him to give the talk to your walking group and explain why it would interest the members.
Propose two possible Saturday dates in spring and ask which one would suit him.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: This week we are looking at how online news sites deal with their audiences. Many sites let readers post comments directly beneath each story, while others have closed these sections and accept responses only in other ways. Before our next class, I would like your view: should online news sites keep reader comment sections open beneath their stories, or is it better to close them? Why?

studentPosts.name: Marta
studentPosts.post: I think comment sections should stay open. Readers often know things the reporter doesn't. Under a story about flooding in my town, residents pointed out that a street name was wrong, and the site corrected it within an hour. Without comments, readers lose their chance to answer back and add local knowledge.

studentPosts.name: Devon
studentPosts.post: I would close them. Comment sections fill up quickly with abusive or misleading remarks, and someone on staff has to spend hours screening them instead of reporting. A letters page, where editors choose a few thoughtful responses to publish, still gives readers a voice without leaving insults sitting right under a serious story.
